title: The repeated bout effect influences lower-extremity biomechanics during a 30-min downhill run
authors: Khassetarash A, Baggaley M, Vernillo G, Millet GY, Edwards WB
population: 11 male participants, two 30-min downhill runs 3 weeks apart at 2.8 m/s and -11.3 degrees
findings: The second bout (DR2) had less MVIC loss (P = 0.004) and less perceived quadriceps pain (P < 0.001) than the first (DR1).
Duty factor increased +5.4% in DR2 versus +8.8% in DR1 (P < 0.035).
Leg stiffness fell 11.7% (P = 0.002) and joint quasi-stiffness up to 25.4% (all P < 0.001) in DR1 but not in DR2.
DR2 involved less energy absorption and generation than DR1 (P < 0.004).
The two bouts were three weeks apart (stated in the highlights); each was 30 min at 2.8 m/s on a -11.3 degree treadmill.
limitations: Eleven male participants, treadmill, fixed slope and speed, a single repeat at one interval. No control group and no follow-up beyond the second bout; the abstract calls the mechanism speculative.
implications: One 30 min downhill bout at -11.3 degrees (tan 11.3 degrees = 0.20, so -20% grade) at 2.8 m/s (10.1 km/h) attenuated muscle-function loss, pain and biomechanical changes when repeated 3 weeks later. A single early exposure about 3 weeks before heavy downhill work is therefore a defensible default, tested at that one interval only.

Unaccustomed runners lose downhill leg stiffness and absorb more energy over 30 min of steep descent. The study used 30 min only, so a safe first-exposure cap is not established; start shorter and progress.

verification.notes: Crossref: Eur J Sport Sci 23(4):510-519, print 2023 (online 2022-03-29), five authors match. Used PubMed XML because Europe PMC text drops the less-than signs from P values; all numbers then supported. Design relabelled repeated-measures (not a crossover).
